metadata.title: Alphabet tumbles 12% on capex: Why Oracle is bucking the tech sell-off

content.text:
Investing.com and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.
Investing.com — Wall Street's tolerance for unchecked artificial intelligence spending broke Wednesday evening. In a sharp post-market divergence, Alphabet sank more than 12% after massive infrastructure outlays drove another quarter of negative free cash flow, while Oracle rallied 10.7% as enterprise demand accelerated across its cloud business.
The contrast highlights a critical turning point for tech: investors are no longer rewarding open-ended capital expenditures—they are demanding immediate returns on invested capital. InvestingPro's screening models track where that cash conversion is actually occurring, evaluating contract backlogs, capacity utilization, and valuation cushions. Ahead of the November rebalance, our strategies are tracking a focused basket of critical infrastructure specialists, enterprise software leaders, and semiconductor enablers quietly turning physical compute demand into booked revenue.
Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ:GOOG) tumbled 12.29% to $288.32 on Thursday as aggressive data center commitments collided with margin scrutiny. In its latest quarterly report, revenue expanded to $127.58 billion, but diluted earnings fell to $2.12 per share. The core drag appeared across the cash flow statement: quarterly investing outlays climbed to $71.35 billion against $42.29 billion in operating cash flow, deepening its free cash flow deficit as management raised full-year capital expenditure guidance to between $195 billion and $205 billion.
While Google Cloud backlog stands at $514 billion and the Gemini app surpassed 950 million active users, the market is no longer giving hyperscalers a blank check. Ballooning hardware depreciation, multi-billion-dollar power commitments—including a 3.6-gigawatt nuclear supply agreement with Constellation Energy—and a federal antitrust monitor overseeing its ad-tech stack are compressing near-term margins. Across 14 financial models, InvestingPro calculates Alphabet's Fair Value at $327.99 per share, but near-term momentum remains trapped until management demonstrates tangible capital discipline.
Accelerating enterprise cloud with 98% GPU utilization
Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) offered the exact counterweight the market demanded, rallying 10.7% to $144.54. While consumer-facing hyperscalers absorb heavy depreciation on unmonetized models, Oracle demonstrated accelerating commercial adoption across enterprise infrastructure.
In its latest quarter, Oracle posted record revenue of $19.35 billion, up 30% year-over-year, alongside non-GAAP earnings of $1.92 per share—beating consensus estimates by 11%. The core growth driver was Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), where revenue surged 121% to $7.4 billion, marking its ninth consecutive quarter of acceleration. Crucially, that physical capacity is already fully absorbed: Oracle delivered 850 megawatts of capacity and over 300,000 GPUs in the quarter, achieving 97.9% GPU utilization while signing contract renewals at a 20% premium.
Oracle is also mitigating capex strain through capital-efficient structuring. Over $30 billion in new AI contracts were closed in the quarter without requiring additional Oracle capital, funded instead through customer prepayments, supplier financing, and bring-your-own-hardware arrangements. Meanwhile, multicloud database revenue exploded 353% year-over-year as Oracle embedded its database architecture across 70 dedicated regions inside AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.
That execution does not eliminate balance-sheet risk. Oracle's full-year capital expenditure guidance of $90 billion to $95 billion contributed to negative free cash flow of $5 billion in its first quarter, while credit default swap spreads briefly neared 300 basis points during mid-October's bond market volatility.
Yet at just 15.5 times forward earnings, the market has priced in substantial skepticism. Across 37 Wall Street analysts, consensus forecasts project earnings expanding to $8.11 this fiscal year and $11.04 in fiscal 2028, giving Oracle an unusually compressed PEG ratio of 0.45 alongside a 13-year dividend growth streak. Investors can see in the Oracle Pro Research Report, the median analyst price target sits at $235.80, pointing to significant upside from current levels.
Focusing on enterprise monetization ahead of November
As the artificial intelligence trade matures, the era of unscrutinized multiple expansion is giving way to disciplined capital evaluation. Companies that merely spend billions on speculative hardware are facing immediate margin compression, while those converting infrastructure demand into contracted enterprise backlog continue to gain ground.
InvestingPro's disciplined screening models systematically track operating margins, capacity monetization, and valuation buffers across the tech landscape. Heading into the November 1st monthly rebalance, our strategies already hold Oracle across both Tech Titans and Beat the S&P 500. The complete roster of top-ranked stocks and the fresh additions dropping in the November update can be accessed directly on InvestingPro.
